Task and constraints: You are given a large integer represented as an integer array digits, where each digits[i] is the i^th digit of the integer. The digits are ordered from most significant to least significant in left-to-right order. The large integer does not contain any leading 0's. The method returns the requested output under the stated constraints.
Idea: Walks digits right to left, turns each 9 into 0, increments the first non-nine and returns; if all are nines, prepends 1.
Technique and why it applies: Carry propagation handles decimal increment directly.
Invariant: Digits to the right are zero after carry passes them.
Edge cases: [9] becomes [1,0]; the input list is modified for ordinary cases.
Complexity: No author label was supplied. Time is O(n) worst case; the all-nine case allocates O(n) output space.

Task and constraints: Given two binary strings a and b, return their sum as a binary string. The method returns the requested output under the stated constraints.
Idea: Processes binary digits from right to left, adding paired bits and carry, and reverses the generated output string at the end.
Technique and why it applies: Manual binary addition handles unequal string lengths and carry without converting the entire values.
Invariant: Each output bit equals the sum of the current input bits and incoming carry modulo two; carry is the remaining quotient.
Edge cases: Inputs may have different lengths; leading zero output is removed or retained depending on the implementation's final join/strip.
Complexity: No author label was supplied. Time and output space are O(max(m,n)) for one pass over the bits.

Task and constraints: Given an array of strings words and a width maxWidth, format the text such that each line has exactly maxWidth characters and is fully (left and right) justified. The method returns the requested output under the stated constraints.
Idea: Greedily packs as many words as fit in each line, then distributes spaces between words; the last line is left-justified and padded to maxWidth.
Technique and why it applies: Greedy line packing is appropriate because words cannot be split and each line must fit the width.
Invariant: Each completed line contains the selected words and exactly maxWidth characters after spacing/padding.
Edge cases: A one-word line receives all remaining spaces; the last line uses single spaces. The code assumes each word fits the width.
Complexity: The author labels time O(n) and space null; the code processes all characters and builds output strings, so O(total input characters plus output) time/space is more accurate.

Task and constraints: Given a non-negative integer x, compute and return the square root of x. The method returns the requested output under the stated constraints.
Idea: Binary-searches a candidate integer root, comparing its square to x and narrowing the interval until the floor square root is found.
Technique and why it applies: Binary search works because integer squares increase monotonically.
Invariant: The search interval continues to contain the floor square root until termination.
Edge cases: x=0 or 1 returns directly if covered by bounds; the returned value is the integer floor, not a floating-point root.
Complexity: No author label was supplied. Time is O(log x) for a bounded integer search and auxiliary space O(1).

Task and constraints: You are climbing a staircase. It takes n steps to reach the top. The method returns the requested output under the stated constraints.
Idea: Uses a memo dictionary for recursive subproblems; each call returns a cached count when available or sums the ways reached by the allowed previous steps.
Technique and why it applies: Memoized recursion avoids recalculating the same stair-count subproblems.
Invariant: A cached entry stores the number of ways for its stair index.
Edge cases: Small n needs base cases; negative or zero n behavior depends on the actual base-case code. Recursion depth can grow with n.
Complexity: No author label was supplied. With memoization, time and space are O(n), including cache and recursion stack.

Task and constraints: Given a string path, which is an absolute path (starting with a slash '/') to a file or directory in a Unix-style file system, convert it to the simplified canonical path. The method returns the requested output under the stated constraints.
Idea: Splits the path on slashes and processes tokens with a stack: empty tokens and '.' are ignored, '..' removes a prior component when possible, and ordinary names are pushed.
Technique and why it applies: A stack models path components because '..' reverses the latest directory component.
Invariant: The stack represents the normalized path components processed so far.
Edge cases: Repeated slashes and '.' do not add components; '..' at root cannot move above root.
Complexity: The author labels O(n) time and O(n) space, consistent with splitting and storing path tokens.

Task and constraints: Given two strings word1 and word2, return the minimum number of operations required to convert word1 to word2. The method returns the requested output under the stated constraints.
Idea: Recursively compares suffixes of the two words, considering deletion, insertion and replacement when characters differ, and memoizes each index pair.
Technique and why it applies: Memoized dynamic programming avoids recomputing edit-distance subproblems.
Invariant: The cached state gives the minimum edits needed for the two remaining suffixes.
Edge cases: Empty suffixes require the remaining length in edits; recursion and memoization cover each index pair.
Complexity: No author label was supplied. Time and space are O(m*n) for the index-pair states, plus recursion depth O(m+n).

Task and constraints: Given two strings word1 and word2, return the minimum number of operations required to convert word1 to word2. The method returns the requested output under the stated constraints.
Idea: Builds a full table of edit distances, initializes the first column and row for deleting or inserting characters, then applies match or minimum of insert/delete/replace.
Technique and why it applies: Two-dimensional dynamic programming models edits between every pair of prefixes.
Invariant: distance[i][j] is the minimum edits converting the first i characters to the first j characters.
Edge cases: Empty words use the initialized boundary row/column; equal characters take the diagonal without added cost.
Complexity: The author labels O(n*m) time and O(n*m) space, consistent with the full table.

Task and constraints: Given two strings word1 and word2, return the minimum number of operations required to convert word1 to word2. The method returns the requested output under the stated constraints.
Idea: Uses a rolling row for edit distance, swapping words so the row is based on the shorter string, and updates each cell from insertion, deletion and substitution costs.
Technique and why it applies: Rolling-row dynamic programming needs only the previous row and current left cell.
Invariant: The previous row describes the prior prefix of one word; the current row is built left to right.
Edge cases: Empty strings reduce to the other word's length; swapping keeps the shorter dimension in memory.
Complexity: The author labels O(n*m) time and O(n+m) space; the code uses O(min(m,n)) row storage plus temporary state.

Task and constraints: Write an efficient algorithm that searches for a value target in an m x n integer matrix matrix. This matrix has the following properties: The method returns the requested output under the stated constraints.
Idea: Binary-searches the matrix as if its rows were concatenated into one sorted array, converting each midpoint index into row and column coordinates.
Technique and why it applies: Binary search fits because each row follows the previous row in sorted order under the stated matrix property.
Invariant: The search interval contains the target's possible flattened index if it exists.
Edge cases: A single cell and target outside the overall range terminate normally; the code assumes a nonempty matrix.
Complexity: No author label was supplied. Time is O(log(m*n)) and auxiliary space O(1).

Task and constraints: Given two strings s and t of lengths m and n respectively, return the minimum window substring of s such that every character in t (including duplicates) is included in the window. If there is no such substring, return the empty string "". The method returns the requested output under the stated constraints.
Idea: Expands a right pointer while counting required characters, then shrinks the left pointer whenever the current window covers the target, saving the shortest valid window.
Technique and why it applies: Sliding window tracks a contiguous substring while frequency counts test whether it covers the target multiset.
Invariant: The window counts reflect the characters between left and right, and the best recorded window is the shortest valid one seen.
Edge cases: If no covering window exists, the code returns an empty string; duplicate target characters require matching counts, not just membership.
Complexity: The author labels time O(n) and space null; the standard frequency-window scan is O(|s|+|t|), with character-count storage O(unique characters).

Task and constraints: Given two integers n and k, return all possible combinations of k numbers chosen from the range [1, n]. The method returns the requested output under the stated constraints.
Idea: Recursively or iteratively chooses increasing integers from 1 through n until k values are selected, then stores each combination.
Technique and why it applies: Backtracking enumerates k-element subsets; increasing choices prevent permutation duplicates.
Invariant: The current path contains strictly increasing selected values and its length never exceeds k.
Edge cases: k=0 yields the empty combination in standard base-case handling; bounds determine whether any choices remain.
Complexity: The author labels O(k*C(n,k)) time and O(k) space, excluding the returned combinations; each output combination has k values.

Task and constraints: Given an integer array nums of unique elements, return all possible subsets (the power set). The method returns the requested output under the stated constraints.
Idea: Generates subsets by either recursion or iterative expansion, adding or excluding each input value and storing each resulting selection.
Technique and why it applies: Subset enumeration considers the two choices for each input element.
Invariant: Each partial subset contains only values from the processed prefix; iterative variants preserve all subsets formed so far.
Edge cases: An empty input yields the empty subset. Duplicate input values can produce duplicate subsets unless a variant explicitly deduplicates.
Complexity: The author labels O(n*2^n) time and O(1) auxiliary space; output itself stores O(n*2^n) elements, and recursion variants use O(n) stack.
